title: REST API Design Principles
learning_outcomes: Explain how rest api design principles affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from consistency and predictability to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on rest api design principles in rest architectural principles. You will connect consistency and predictability to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: REST API Design Principles matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying consistency and predictability deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Lesson 28 concept map
content_blocks.alt_text: Lesson 28: Consistency and predictability → Resource-oriented modeling → Explicit behavior and contracts → Simplicity and evolvability.
content_blocks.caption: Follow the 4 syllabus topics in order, then inspect the example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: REST is an architectural style with constraints; an HTTP JSON API can be useful without satisfying every REST constraint. In this lesson, treat “REST API Design Principles” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to connect
items: REST describes constraints, not a wire protocol

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: REST API Design Principles
content_blocks.code:
GET /v1/orders/ord_123 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.test
Accept: application/json

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"ord_123","status":"processing"}
content_blocks.expected_output: The identifier names a resource and the response transfers one representation of its current state.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Consistency and predictability”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Resource-oriented modeling” and “Simplicity and evolvability”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Describe the architectural choice precisely; do not call every JSON endpoint strict REST. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating rest api design principles. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Consistency and predictability” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for REST API Design Principles with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating rest api design principles as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: REST is an architectural style with constraints; an HTTP JSON API can be useful without satisfying every REST constraint. In this lesson, treat “REST API Design Principles” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 29: Identifying Resources from Business Requirements.
